title: What will Gamaliel Cordoba, Marcos’ newest SC pick, bring to Padre Faura?
summary: Cordoba was the NTC commissioner when the Duterte administration launched a crackdown against ABS-CBN and Bulatlat. He also has ties with a big fishing company.

items: Gamaliel Asis Cordoba was appointed as the third associate justice of the Supreme Court by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in November 2023, following his tenure as chairperson of the Commission on Audit (COA).

During his time at COA, Cordoba oversaw significant financial audits, including the disallowance of confidential funds for Vice President Sara Duterte's office, and faced criticism for delays in publishing Annual Audit Reports.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Gamaliel Asis Cordoba entered President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration in 2022 when Commission on Audit (COA) chairperson Jose Calida resigned just months into his post.

On November 13, Cordoba’s strong ties with Marcos became apparent again after the President picked him as his third appointee to the Supreme Court (SC). Cordoba replaced former associate justice Amy Lazaro Javier, an appointee of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who retired on November 16.

He is the latest Marcos appointee to the High Court after Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025, and recently, Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on November 5. He is the country’s 196th SC associate justice.

This brings the number of Marcos appointees to the High Court to three, compared with two appointed by the late former president Benigno Aquino III and nine by former president Rodrigo Duterte. Zalameda’s appointment as chief justice leaves another vacancy in the associate justice post.

Cordoba served for four years and a month in COA, the government institution mandated to audit government finances and purchases. In 2022 and 2023, he was external auditor of the International Labour Organization.

Under Cordoba, COA issued a notice of disallowance on Vice President Sara Duterte’s P73-million confidential funds for the Office of the Vice President (OVP), and P75 million for the Department of Education (DepEd)
While COA has already cleared the DepEd funds, it affirmed with finality the disallowance against the OVP. (READ: With finality: COA affirms disallowance of Sara Duterte’s P73-M confidential funds)

It was also under Cordoba in 2024 when the commission started delaying the publication of its Annual Audit Reports or AAR. Budget transparency advocates, journalists, and even politicians rely on AARs to check how agencies used their funds and if there are red flags from these transactions.
Advocates criticized the delay in publication, asserting that it neither indicated transparency nor established credibility.

blocks.caption: COA delays publishing of audit reports. How can this affect us?

blocks.text: Cordoba was the longest serving commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) — from 2009 to 2022.
He was the NTC commissioner when former president Duterte waged a campaign against media giant ABS-CBN that ultimately led to the network’s shutdown.

At the height of the controversy, Cordoba said in one of the legislative inquiries in 2020 that the NTC would “most likely” issue a provisional authority so ABS-CBN could continue operating pending a franchise renewal. Cordoba also said at the time that ABS-CBN had no standing penalties with the NTC.
But ABS-CBN’s franchise expired and was not renewed during Duterte’s term. Its shutdown led to the retrenchment of around 5,000 personnel.
When Cordoba was still with the NTC, the website of alternative news site Bulatlat was also blocked.

Before the end of Duterte’s term in 2022, then-national security adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr. wrote to Cordoba, requesting the commission to “order Philippine Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to block access to the following websites affiliated [with] and are supporting these terrorists and terrorist organizations.”
Esperon used the highly contested anti-terror law to justify the request. He also cited affiliations with terrorist organizations without providing substantial evidence.
After a legal battle, Bulatlat’s website was unblocked after the news site won against the NTC and Esperon in court.
But this was not the only issue that Cordoba got embroiled in.

A Rappler investigation in 2024 showed that the family of Cordoba’s wife, Monica Elena Cordoba, partly owns the commercial fishing company Mercidar Fishing Corporation. A copy of Cordoba’s 2023 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth obtained by Rappler showed that he was also a shareholder of Mercidar in 2015 and 2019 — the years when he was already with the NTC.

To avoid conflicts of interest, Section 9 of the Code of Conduct for Public Officials requires officials to divest themselves of their shareholdings or financial interest within 60 days of taking office. Rappler found that during Cordoba’s time in the NTC, the commission stopped issuing service numbers for trackers that would prevent unregulated fishing.
Mercidar is central to the municipal waters issue. Originally, 15-kilometer municipal waters were exclusively for small fisherfolk.

But in December 2023, Malabon City Regional Trial Court Judge Zaldy Docena allowed Mercidar to operate within the 15-kilometer municipal waters except in shallow waters (less than 7 fathoms deep). A year later, in 2024, the SC affirmed this decision.

blocks.caption: Top officials with private interests spoil effort to track big fishers

blocks.text: Although not a politician, Cordoba has proven to be somewhat of a political survivor, having served under four presidents: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Aquino, Duterte, and Marcos.
Arroyo appointed him in 2009, and the succeeding presidents kept him as part of their administrations until his appointment to the COA, an independent body.

His COA profile claimed that Cordoba’s stint in the NTC saw the improvement in the country’s internet connectivity. It also said that under him, the NTC broke the long-time duopoly in the country’s telecommunications industry.

“The country’s fixed broadband and mobile internet speeds remarkably improved globally under his leadership with Ookla Speedtest Global Index now ranking the Philippines 41st out of 180 countries globally for fixed broadband and 79th out of 140 countries for mobile,” said Cordoba’s profile.

“… The NTC broke the long-time duopoly in the telecommunications industry by successfully selecting a third telco through a most transparent bidding process under the guidance of the International Telecommunication Union,” it added.
Cordoba is a government official through and through. In 2010, Arroyo gave him the Presidential Medal of Merit “for his exemplary performance and service delivery to the Filipino people.”
He has also held the following positions in government:

items: director of the Office of Presidential Chief of Staff (2001-2002)
appointments secretary, Office of the President (2006-2007)
member of board of directors, Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (2008-2009)

blocks.text: Before joining government, Cordoba worked as an associate lawyer at Siguion Reyna, Montecillo and Ongsiako Law Offices. He also worked as a tax lawyer at accounting firm SyCip Gorres Velayo and Co.

The new SC associate justice joined the long list of High Court magistrates who are products of the Ateneo de Manila University. He earned his economics degree from the university in 1992, then his juris doctor four years later. Cordoba passed the Bar in 1997 with Roll No. 42213.
Like Zalameda, Cordoba is a member of the Fraternal Order of Utopia.

blocks.text: To secure his SC appointment, Cordoba had to beat other strong contenders.

Some of the shortlisted nominees for the post have been serving in the judiciary for decades, or are respected lawyers like Solicitor General Darlene Marie Berberabe, whom Marcos did not pick in the last two selections for SC justice.
Cordoba applied only once and got the job.

blocks.caption: Who are the candidates short-listed for SC associate justice?

blocks.text: During his Judicial and Bar Council interview on October 13, Cordoba said he applied for the position because he felt like it was the “time” to seek higher office. He said he believed it was his chance to affect more people and have a lasting legacy in public service.

Given his experience with mainly executive offices, the new justice said he would bring to the SC en banc a different perspective in handling cases. He said he believed that while having judicial experience was an advantage for an associate justice, his executive experience was something that should be considered too.
“We’re bringing many facets and many fresh new ideas which we can inject into the decisions,” he said.

As an associate justice, Cordoba promised to support the SC’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations or SPJI. He said the program has to continue and be expanded even more, adding that the initiative brings the courts closer to people.
SPJI is the brainchild of former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo that introduced innovations in the judiciary, including digitalization. The project has been running since 2022 and will end in 2027.

blocks.caption: What will Gamaliel Cordoba, Marcos’ newest SC pick, bring to Padre Faura?

blocks.text: As an SC justice, Cordoba said he would be the type who would follow what’s written in the 1987 Constitution and existing jurisprudence. He said he would act according to the Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability.
Cordoba also said he would inhibit himself if cases he participated in under the NTC, COA, and related offices found their way to the Supreme Court. – Rappler.com
